An Advanced Empirical Remote Sensing and Machine-Readable Cartographic Intelligence Platform

Department of Geoinformatics, Shivaji University, Kolhapur

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
The Latur District Near Real-Time Drought Monitoring System is an open-source, operational scientific platform developed to provide continuous, high-resolution drought surveillance across 954 villages and 10 tehsils in the drought-vulnerable Marathwada region of Maharashtra, India.

Integrating multi-sensor Earth Observation constellations—including Copernicus Sentinel-2 MSI (optical vegetation condition), Sentinel-1 C-SAR (root-zone soil moisture), Landsat 8/9 TIRS (land surface temperature), and UCSB CHIRPS (satellite-gauge precipitation)—the system computes standardized multi-scale hydrological indicators and fuses them into a transparent, rule-grounded Composite Drought Index (CDI).

docs.title: Why Latur Demands Continuous Village-Level Surveillance
docs.text:
1. Rain-Shadow Semiarid Climatology: Latur lies on the leeward side of the Western Ghats, receiving an erratic mean annual rainfall of 750–800 mm, with \(>85\%\) concentrated during the southwest monsoon (June–September).
  2. Heavy Vertisol Soils (Black Cotton Soils): Agriculture predominantly relies on rainfed deep vertisols. While these soils exhibit high moisture retention capacity, prolonged dry spells during the Kharif flowering phase (August–September) cause rapid moisture depletion, soil cracking, and root shearing.
  3. Historical Drought Emergencies: In 2015–2016, Latur suffered one of India's most catastrophic municipal water crises, requiring the deployment of the Jaldoot water trains to deliver drinking water to Latur city. Subsequent agricultural crises in 2018–2019 devastated Kharif soybean and pulse yields.
  4. Administrative Granularity: The district is partitioned into 10 administrative tehsils encompassing 954 revenue villages. Broad tehsil-averaged rainfall statistics frequently conceal acute micro-watershed crop failures. This system delivers village-level resolution (\(10\text{--}20\text{ m}\) effective spatial scale).

docs.title: Data accuracy audit and pipeline repair (October 2026)
docs.text: What was checked, what was wrong, what was changed, and what is still open. Every number below was measured on the files in this repository.

docs.title: 1. Village count: 954 vs 951
docs.text:
The polygons are 954. The dashboard served 951 histories because village_timeseries.json, village_baselines.json and villages_by_tehsil.json were keyed by tehsil::village-name, and three pairs of villages share a name inside one tehsil:

Tehsil Name Polygon ids Ahmadpur Anandwadi 4, 5 Chakur Hatkarwadi 293, 294 Nilanga Kamshetwadi 642, 643

One polygon of each pair was drawn with its namesake's numbers. Fixed by keying everything on the polygon id: scripts/analysis/build_village_timeseries.py, scripts/analysis/build_village_registry.py, the map, sidebar, drawer, timeseries page and /api/v1/timeseries?id=. The dropdown selects by id, so two "Anandwadi" entries are two selectable villages. scripts/tests/test_pipeline.py fails if the count ever drifts again.

docs.title: 2. Legends that did not match the map
docs.text:
• The map painted CDI with the US-DM palette (None = white), while the legend swatches were green / yellow / amber. SPI polygons used cut-offs (-0.5, -1.0, -1.5, -2.0) that disagree with classify.py (-0.5, -0.8, -1.3, -1.6, -2.0).
  • NDVI, VCI, VHI and rainfall layers showed the CDI legend ("None, D0 ... D4").
  • The compare and timelapse pages classified every index with the SPI function, so an NDVI of 0.3 was coloured as "no drought".
  • The sidebar re-derived the drought class from 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6 / 0.8 instead of 0.20 / 0.35 / 0.50 / 0.65 / 0.80, so the sidebar and the map could disagree on the same village.

Now frontend/lib/metrics.ts is the only place a layer's bins, colours and labels are defined; the fill colour, legend, tooltip, compare/timelapse pages and sidebar all read it. The legend also shows how many villages fall in each bin for the month on screen and says so when a layer has no data. Tests compare the TypeScript palette and thresholds against classify.py and config/composite.yaml. The "no drought" colour changed from white to sage because white was invisible on a light basemap.

docs.title: 3. Baseline drought maps
docs.text: village_baselines.json existed but nothing mapped it. New layers, group "Baseline": normal NDVI for the month, normal rainfall for the month, NDVI departure (z-score), rainfall as a percentage of normal. Definitions follow baseline_drought_architecture.md section 2 (per-village, per-calendar-month mean and standard deviation over 2016-2026). The legend's "defn" button states each layer's definition.

docs.title: 4. Are the backend indices right for each village?
docs.text:
Check Result SPI-1/3/6/12 recomputed from the village rain table (Thom gamma, Stagge zero-centre) vs stored SPI correlation 0.9999 to 1.0000, mean abs. difference 0.002 to 0.006. SPI arithmetic is correct. Village CDI recomputed from the stored inputs and config/composite.yaml identical to the stored value (max diff 0.0) Village PCI recomputed identical Class vs score in the served time series 73 of 75,068 rows disagree, all within rounding of a threshold

Problems that are real and not fixed here, because fixing them changes published numbers and needs the team's decision (AGENTS.md rule 2):

  1. EVI is wrong at source. The zonal EVI has median exactly 1.0; 20 % of village-months equal 1.0 and 16 % exceed 1.0 (max 1.38). build_baseline_drought.py then silently clips to [-1, 1], hiding it. Its own comment says "DN not scaled by 10000". EVI carries weight 0.10 in the CDI. The dashboard no longer offers EVI as a map layer; the real-time job withholds EVI from new months. Rebuild EVI from the rasters with the reflectance scale fixed.
  2. VHI equals VCI in 100 % of rows (no thermal band, documented in build_village_indices.py). With weights VHI 0.20 + VCI 0.15 the same signal carries 35 % of the composite, and it makes the min_inputs: 3 rule easy to satisfy. Either drop VHI from the composite or build it as 0.5 VCI + 0.5 PCI as memory.md defines.
  3. Rainfall is sampled at the village centroid on a ~5 km grid. The rain used for PCI has about 263 distinct values across 954 villages in a month (a village's rain is the value of the CHIRPS cell holding its centroid), and the rain used for SPI has about 700. They are two different samplings of the same data. Neighbouring villages therefore share one number and cliffs appear at cell edges. This is the main reason a village's rainfall can look wrong against ground knowledge. A polygon zonal mean computed once from the CHIRPS rasters for both PCI and SPI would fix the inconsistency (it cannot be rebuilt from this repository: the rasters are not committed).
  4. SPI is calibrated on 2016-2026 only (about 10 values per calendar month). The status file used to claim "1991-2020". It now states the real reference. With so few values the gamma fit is rough; values beyond +/-2 deserve caution. Fetching CHIRPS 1991-2020 from Earth Engine and fitting on that is the standard remedy.
  5. The CDI class is sensitive to the short record. Each village-month is judged against the median and MAD of about 7 values. Scoring a month against a reference that excludes the month itself reproduces the stored class for 89-100 % of villages in most months, but only 63 % for October 2026. Treat single-month class flips as uncertain.
  6. Three Sentinel-2 filename conventions are radiometrically inconsistent (corrected with a per-batch additive offset, estimate_offsets in build_village_indices.py). New months come from Earth Engine S2_SR_HARMONIZED, a different processing chain; a bias check against the historic NDVI over an overlapping month should be run on the first live data.
  7. Monsoon gaps. 22 of 98 Sentinel-2 months have a composite for fewer than half of the villages (June to September in most years). The map shows them as "no data" and the legend counts them.
  8. CHIRPS stops at 2026-08. 2026-09 and 2026-10 have no rainfall, SPI or PCI, so their CDI uses only NDVI, VCI and VHI (which equals VCI). The home page shows input completeness for the month.

docs.title: 5. Real-time pipeline
docs.text:
Why it never worked on GitHub Actions, in the order it fails:

  1. chirps_gee.py and pipeline_gee.py default to data/vector/latur_tehsils.geojson; the folder contains only .gitkeep, so both exit with "AOI not found".
  2. chirps_gee.py called ee.Initialize() with no credentials and fell back to the interactive ee.Authenticate(), which hangs a CI job. It also read UCSB-CHG/CHIRPS/monthly, which Earth Engine does not publish (only DAILY and PENTAD), and tested img is None on a server-side object.
  3. build_village_indices.py needs rasterio and local rasters, neither on the runner. The workflow treated that failure as "expected".
  4. run_realtime_pipeline_sync.py ignored every failed step, never wrote the new month into village_timeseries.json or the village GeoJSON, overwrote latest_status.json with monitoring_status: "operational" and both sources "operational" regardless of outcome, and inserted a hard-coded Supabase row (village "Latur", cloud 5.2 %, SPI-1 copied from SPI-3).
  5. The workflow did not install pyyaml (imported at module load), did not pass the period input, and always printed "SUCCESS".
  6. /api/v1/realtime and /api/v1/realtime/validate returned constants: "operational", "latest period 2026-10", "96.25 % accuracy", "954 boundaries with 0 gaps".
  7. The header showed a pulsing green "Live Sentinel-2 - GEE Operational" at all times.
  8. latest_status.json was not in frontend/public/data, so the status route always fell back to a placeholder.

What replaced it: scripts/realtime/realtime_update.py (details in its docstring and .github/workflows/realtime_drought_sync.yml).

  • Village-level Sentinel-2 NDVI and CHIRPS rainfall from Earth Engine, month by month, oldest first; a CHIRPS month is used only when every daily image is published.
  • SPI recomputed for all four scales; before writing, the job recomputes SPI on the stored history and aborts if it drifts from the stored values.
  • VCI/VHI/PCI/CDI computed with config/composite.yaml against the existing record; history is not rewritten. Scoring an existing month reproduces its stored score exactly (tested).
  • A month whose Sentinel-2 arrived before its rainfall is re-scored when the rainfall lands, which is exactly the 2026-09 / 2026-10 situation today.
  • Rebuilds the history file, baselines, district series and latest GeoJSON.
  • latest_status.json records what happened. The job exits non-zero when a due month produced nothing; the workflow still commits the status so the site shows "Behind" or "Incomplete" rather than a stale "operational", then fails the run.
  • The status chip, /api/v1/realtime and /api/v1/realtime/validate now read the real files; the validator computes its checks from the served data.

Not verified here: no Earth Engine credentials were available in this environment, so the two fetch functions (fetch_s2, fetch_chirps) have not been run against the live service. Everything after them was exercised end to end with --fixture (rain for 2026-09 and 2026-10 plus a synthetic 2026-11): 954 villages scored, SPI tables extended, history left identical, status written. Run python scripts/realtime/realtime_update.py --period 2026-09 once with the service account to confirm.

docs.title: 6. Other fixes
docs.text:
• Upload page posted to /upload/aoi, a route that does not exist in the Next.js app. The AOI is now analysed in the browser (GeoJSON in EPSG:4326): drawn on the map, intersected with the 954 villages, area-weighted CDI, class split, village table, CSV download.
  • Tehsil and district outlines were interactive polygons stacked above the villages and could swallow hover/click events; they are now inert panes. Cursor: open hand on the map, pointer only over a village. Tooltips no longer follow the cursor.
  • Overlaps: basemap picker and control bar shared the same corner; the legend and timeline shared the bottom edge; the village drawer covered the page header. Legend and timeline now sit in one dock, controls in separate slots, the drawer inside the map frame.
  • The Google tile URLs (mt1.google.com) are not an authorised tile API. The default basemap is now a plain CARTO light map; Google entries remain selectable, review before a public launch.
  • Removed the sidebar "Official Government Drought Zone Notice" with fixed counts (490 / 228); it is now a sentence computed from the villages on screen.

docs.title: 7. Published accuracy figures that cannot be reproduced from this repository
docs.text: docs/README.md and docs/VALIDATION_AND_ACCURACY_REPORT.md state a hit rate of 94.21 %, false-alarm ratio 5.76 %, CSI 0.8906 and overall accuracy 96.25 %, from "28,450 of 30,200 actual drought crises" matched to "government declarations / relief dispatches". The repository contains no ground-truth dataset and no script that computes these metrics; the only code that mentioned them was the hard-coded /api/v1/realtime/validate response, now removed. The same reports describe 951 villages, a CDI of 0.50 PCI + 0.25 VCI + 0.25 TCI and a TCI band that does not exist in the pipeline (the real composite is in config/composite.yaml). Until the underlying declaration data and the scoring script are added, do not quote these numbers externally.

docs.title: 1. Raw Data Reality & Audit against drought_image_availability.xlsx
docs.text: To address all discrepancies and ensure complete transparency, the dataset distinguishes between two distinct scientific observation sources:

docs.title: 1.1 The Optical Sentinel-2 Image Record (drought_image_availability.xlsx)
docs.text:
• Total Valid Months: 83 high-quality, cloud-free observation months across 2016–2026 (plus partial seasonal extensions up to 98 observation months in drought_monitoring_master.csv).
  • Missing or Cloud-Obscured Months (Skipped as per drought_image_availability.xlsx):
  • 2016: Months 2, 6, 7, 9 (cloud cover / no pass)
  • 2017: Month 6 (cloud cover)
  • 2018: Month 3, and months 6–12 (cloud cover / faint ticks)
  • 2021: Month 8 (cloud cover mark cc)
  • 2024: Months 6, 7, 8 (monsoon cloud cover mark cc — strictly skipped)
  • 2026: Months 7, 8 (cloud cover mark cc)
  • Scientific Treatment: When optical satellite data is unavailable due to dense monsoon cloud cover or missing orbits, we NEVER fabricate or interpolate NDVI/VCI. They are left as null or marked pending in accordance with Rule §2.4 of AGENTS.md.

docs.title: 1.2 The Continuous CHIRPS Precipitation Record (128 Months)
docs.text:
• Coverage: Continuous monthly rainfall and SPI data across all 128 months from January 2016 through August 2026.
  • Temporal Integrity: Infrared and gauge-blended microwave precipitation records are unobstructed by clouds. Therefore, every village in Latur has 100% continuous monthly SPI-1, SPI-3, SPI-6, and SPI-12 data, even during the cloudy monsoon months of 2016, 2018, 2021, and 2024.
  • Village-Level Verified Table: Extracted and verified from the user's verified record data/processed/csv/SPI1_village_monthly_verified.csv (225 cadastral rows across 128 monthly columns 2016-01 to 2026-08), matching village records such as Ahmadpur (M Cl):

docs.title: 3. Climatological Baselines Formulation & Proof
docs.text: Drought is scientifically defined as a standardized negative anomaly from normal climatology (\(Z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\)). The baseline tables in frontend/public/data/village_baselines.json and data/processed/csv/village_with_baseline.csv were computed as follows:

docs.title: 3.1 Empirical Formulas
docs.text:
For each calendar month \(m \in \{1, 2, \dots, 12\}\) and each cadastral village \(v\):

\[\mu_{v, m} = \frac{1}{N_{v, m}} \sum_{y \in \text{valid years}} X_{v, y, m}\] \[\sigma_{v, m} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{v, m} - 1} \sum_{y \in \text{valid years}} (X_{v, y, m} - \mu_{v, m})^2}\]

Where \(N_{v, m}\) is the count of valid historical observations for that calendar month. For Sentinel-2, only the verified 83 cloud-free months are included in \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). For CHIRPS, all 10 years (2016–2026) are included.

docs.title: Near-Real-Time Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
Status note (October 2026). This document describes the intended architecture. The job that actually runs is scripts/realtime/realtime_update.py; what it does, and what was broken before, is in DATA_ACCURACY_AUDIT.md. In particular: SPI is calibrated on the 2016-2026 record, village polygons are processed directly (not tehsils), and the workflow file is .github/workflows/realtime_drought_sync.yml.

Google Earth Engine (GEE) + PostGIS + Vercel Serverless Sensors: Copernicus Sentinel-2 L2A (10 m) + UCSB CHIRPS v2.0 (~5 km) + Landsat 8/9 LST (30 m) + Sentinel-1 VV Execution Runtime: Python 3.11 / GitHub Actions / Vercel Edge

docs.title: 2. Decoupled Cloud Credentials & GitHub Secrets
docs.text: In compliance with enterprise security requirements, zero secrets or project identifiers are hardcoded into scripts:

docs.title: Required Environment Variables:
docs.text:
• GEE_PROJECT: Google Earth Engine Cloud Project ID (e.g. your Google Cloud project identifier).
  • GEE_PROJECT_NUMBER: Numeric project identifier for service account bindings.
  • DATABASE_URL: Direct PostgreSQL connection string to Supabase PostGIS.
  • SUPABASE_URL: Supabase project URL (https://<project-id>.supabase.co).
  • SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY: Server-side service key for database and storage writes.

docs.title: Adding as GitHub Secrets:
docs.text:
1. Navigate to your GitHub Repository -> Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions.
  2. Add GEE_PROJECT, DATABASE_URL, and SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY.
  3. GitHub Actions automated workflow (.github/workflows/drought_pipeline.yml) runs the ingestion on a scheduled cron or on-demand without exposing credentials.

docs.title: 3.1 Sentinel-2 Cloud Masking
docs.text: Cloud and shadow contamination is masked using the 10 m Scene Classification Layer (SCL): - Masked Pixel Codes: 3 (Cloud Shadow), 8 (Cloud Medium Probability), 9 (Cloud High Probability), 10 (Cirrus), 11 (Snow/Ice). - Composite Method: Monthly medoid / median reducer across cloud-free pixels.

docs.title: 3.2 Spectral Formulas
docs.text:
• NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index): $\(\text{NDVI} = \frac{B_8 - B_4}{B_8 + B_4}\)$
  • EVI (Enhanced Vegetation Index — atmospheric blue correction): $\(\text{EVI} = 2.5 \times \frac{B_8 - B_4}{B_8 + 6.0 \cdot B_4 - 7.5 \cdot B_2 + 1.0}\)$
  • NDMI (Normalized Difference Moisture Index — canopy water content): $\(\text{NDMI} = \frac{B_8 - B_{11}}{B_8 + B_{11}}\)$
  • VCI (Vegetation Condition Index — Kogan 1995): $\(\text{VCI} = 100 \times \frac{\text{NDVI} - \text{NDVI}_{\min}}{\text{NDVI}_{\max} - \text{NDVI}_{\min}}\)$
  • VHI (Vegetation Health Index): $\(\text{VHI} = 0.5 \times \text{VCI} + 0.5 \times \text{TCI}\)$

docs.title: 4. Serverless Vector & Tile Rendering on Vercel
docs.text: Because the platform is deployed on Vercel, traditional heavy spatial servers (such as GeoServer or standalone GIS daemons) are not needed: 1. Cadastral Vector Polygons: Verified Survey of India village polygons are stored as optimized GeoJSON in public/data/latur_villages_latest.geojson. 2. Dynamic In-Browser Styling: Leaflet applies WMO SPI and CDI color scales client-side in sub-milliseconds based on the active timeline scrubber period. 3. GEE Live Tiles: When full-resolution raster layers are requested, GEE returns a signed tile URL template (https://earthengine.googleapis.com/v1/{mapid}/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}) which Leaflet mounts directly as a raster TileLayer. 4. Edge API Route: Next.js App Router route handler at app/api/v1/[...slug]/route.ts handles all /api/v1 calls serverlessly on Vercel with zero cold-start delay.

docs.title: Runbook: run the pipeline, update the results, schedule it
docs.text: For a local coding agent (Antigravity) that has the Earth Engine and Supabase credentials. Do the steps in order and stop at the first failure; report the exact error. Do not edit the pipeline code to make a step pass, and do not use --fixture or any invented data.

GEE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY=<JSON text of the service-account key, or a path to the .json file>

python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'scripts'); from common.gee import init_ee; ee=init_ee(); print(ee.Number(1).add(1).getInfo())"

python scripts/realtime/check_outputs.py
Expected: a month is ingested only when its sources fully cover it, so a recent month can legitimately be skipped ("not fully published"). That is correct. Report which months were ingested, which were skipped and why, and the final status line. Do not force a month that was skipped.

docs.title: 5. Thermal and soil-moisture history (Landsat LST, Sentinel-1 VV)
docs.text:
This calls Earth Engine once per month from 2016 and can take hours; it is resumable.

python scripts/realtime/backfill_thermal.py
COMPOSITE_CONFIG=config/composite_thermal.yaml python scripts/analysis/rescore_panel.py
python scripts/analysis/compare_formulas.py
Report the thermal coverage printed by rescore_panel.py, the output of compare_formulas.py, and any months the backfill skipped. Then run python scripts/realtime/check_outputs.py with COMPOSITE_CONFIG=config/composite_thermal.yaml.

Do not switch the scheduled job to the thermal formula. Switching changes every published class and needs the project team's review of the comparison first. Keep COMPOSITE_CONFIG unset until they approve.

docs.title: 7. Schedule it
docs.text:
The job is incremental and safe to repeat; weekly is enough (all sources are monthly).

Linux / macOS / WSL (cron): 

crontab -e
17 3 * * 1  cd /path/to/repo && ./scripts/realtime/run_scheduled.sh >> logs/cron.log 2>&1
(Mondays 03:17.) The script reads .env, runs the tests, the update and the output checks, writes logs/pipeline_<timestamp>.log, and exits non-zero on any failure.

Windows (Task Scheduler), from an elevated PowerShell: 

$a = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute "powershell.exe" `
     -Argument "-NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File D:\path\to\repo\scripts\run_scheduled.ps1"
$t = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Weekly -DaysOfWeek Monday -At 3:17am
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName "DroughtPipeline" -Action $a -Trigger $t -StartWhenAvailable
Use -StartWhenAvailable so a missed run executes when the machine is next on.

Instead of a local schedule: .github/workflows/realtime_drought_sync.yml runs weekly in GitHub Actions once the secrets GEE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY, SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and the variable GEE_PROJECT are set. Use one scheduler, not both.

docs.text:
• logs/ has the run log; exit code 0 means update and checks passed.
  • The dashboard status bar shows the last Sentinel-2 / CHIRPS month and the time of the last run; it turns red after 10 days without a run.
  • select * from pipeline_runs order by started_at desc limit 5; lists runs and their steps.

docs.title: 1.1 Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI)
docs.text: The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) isolates precipitation anomalies across selected accumulation windows (1, 3, 6, and 12 months) independent of seasonal variations.

docs.title: Step 1: Probability Density Fitting
docs.text:
Precipitation totals \(x\) for a specific calendar month across the baseline period (1991–2020) are modelled via the two-parameter Gamma distribution:

\[g(x) = \frac{1}{\beta^\alpha \Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-x/\beta} \quad \text{for } x > 0\]

Where \(\alpha > 0\) is the shape parameter, \(\beta > 0\) is the scale parameter, and \(\Gamma(\alpha)\) is the gamma function:

\[\Gamma(\alpha) = \int_0^\infty t^{\alpha - 1} e^{-t} dt\]

docs.title: Step 2: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (Thom, 1958)
docs.text: \[\alpha = \frac{1}{4A} \left(1 + \sqrt{1 + \frac{4A}{3}}\right), \quad \text{where } A = \ln(\bar{x}) - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \ln(x_i)}{n}\] \[\beta = \frac{\bar{x}}{\alpha}\]

docs.title: Step 3: Zero-Rainfall Correction (Stagge et al., 2015)
docs.text:
In semi-arid regions such as Marathwada, dry months often have \(x = 0\). The probability of zero precipitation is \(q = \frac{m}{n}\) (where \(m\) is the number of zero-precipitation observations). The cumulative distribution \(H(x)\) is formulated as:

\[H(x) = q + (1 - q) G(x)\]

To prevent truncation bias and maintain zero-centered symmetry, the unbiased center-probability correction is applied:

\[H(0) = \frac{q}{2}\]

docs.title: Step 4: Inverse Normal Transformation
docs.text:
The cumulative probability \(H(x)\) is mapped to the standard normal distribution \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) using the Abramowitz and Stegun (1965) rational approximation:

\[\text{SPI} = -\left(t - \frac{c_0 + c_1 t + c_2 t^2}{1 + d_1 t + d_2 t^2 + d_3 t^3}\right) \quad \text{for } 0 < H(x) \le 0.5\]

Where \(t = \sqrt{\ln\left(\frac{1}{(H(x))^2}\right)}\), and the standard constants are: - \(c_0 = 2.515517, \quad c_1 = 0.802853, \quad c_2 = 0.010328\) - \(d_1 = 1.432788, \quad d_2 = 0.189269, \quad d_3 = 0.001308\)

When \(H(x) > 0.5\), the complement \(1 - H(x)\) is substituted, and the sign of SPI is inverted.

docs.title: 1.2 Remote Sensing Vegetation Condition Index (VCI)
docs.text:
Per Kogan (1995), raw NDVI is confounded by soil background, terrain, and ecological variation. VCI removes local ecological bias by standardizing the current NDVI relative to its historical minimum and maximum for the same location and calendar week/month:

\[\text{VCI} = 100 \times \frac{\text{NDVI} - \text{NDVI}_{\min}}{\text{NDVI}_{\max} - \text{NDVI}_{\min}}\]
  • \(\text{VCI} < 20\%\): Extreme agricultural drought.
  • \(20\% \le \text{VCI} \le 35\%\): Severe vegetative stress (IMD 2016 statutory trigger).
  • \(35\% < \text{VCI} \le 50\%\): Moderate vegetative stress.
  • \(\text{VCI} > 50\%\): Favorable canopy biomass.

docs.title: 1.3 Composite Drought Index (CDI) & Why Machine Learning Was Retired
The Problem with Black-Box Classifiers:
docs.text: Earlier versions of agricultural drought monitoring often attempted to use Random Forest or Neural Network classifiers to predict drought labels. In administrative, statutory, and relief contexts, this approach was retired for three scientific reasons: 1. Lack of Interpretability: An algorithm cannot explain to a district collector or relief commissioner why a specific village was classified as D2 instead of D1. 2. Training Bias & Overfitting: Learned models trained on sparse relief declarations overfit to administrative relief decisions rather than biophysical reality. 3. Imputation Hazards: Machine learning models fail when satellite scenes are cloud-covered (e.g. during July monsoon storms), forcing synthetic zero-filling which produces phantom droughts.

docs.title: The Verified Transparent Solution:
docs.text: Per European Drought Observatory (EDO) and config/composite.yaml: 1. Every component is standardized into a \(0 \dots 1\) drought intensity signal (\(S_i \in [0, 1]\), where \(1 = \text{extreme stress}\)): - For SPI: \(S_{\text{SPI}} = \text{clip}\left(-\frac{\text{SPI}}{3}, 0, 1\right)\) - For Vegetation/Precipitation indices: Robust Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) Z-score: $\(Z_i = \frac{x_i - \text{median}_i}{1.4826 \times \text{MAD}_i}, \quad S_i = \text{clip}\left(-\frac{Z_i}{3}, 0, 1\right)\)$ 2. Weighted Linear Combination: $\(\text{CDI} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \text{Available}} w_i S_i}{\sum_{i \in \text{Available}} w_i}\)$ 3. Missing components are excluded from both numerator and denominator. 4. If fewer than 3 indices are available, the result is explicitly marked pending, ensuring zero spurious data.

docs.title: 2. Empirical Verification Results (Latur Database Audit)
docs.text:
Audit execution on outputs/Dashboard/drought_monitoring_master.csv (94,473 cadastral records):

  1. Precipitation Anomaly & SPI Correlation: $\(r(\text{Rainfall}, \text{SPI-3}) = +0.1565\)$ Confirms precipitation totals directly calibrate the agricultural SPI scale.

  2. Crop Canopy Response: $\(r(\text{SPI-3}, \text{NDVI}) = +0.2037\)$ Statistically validates that vegetative greenness contracts during rainfall deficits.

  3. Composite Scoring Fidelity: $\(r(\text{SPI-3}, \text{CDI}) = -0.6445\)$ Strong negative correlation, proving that lower SPI values (dryness) reliably produce higher CDI scores (drought severity).

docs.title: Land-surface temperature, soil moisture, TCI and VHI
docs.text: Near Real-Time Drought Monitoring System, Department of Geoinformatics, Shivaji University.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The first version had no thermal band: VHI was set equal to VCI, so one vegetation signal carried 35 % of the composite and nothing measured heat stress or soil water. Kogan's VHI needs both halves:

VHI = 0.5 * VCI + 0.5 * TCI          TCI = 100 * (LSTmax - LST) / (LSTmax - LSTmin)

and agricultural drought is better described by soil moisture than by rainfall alone.

docs.title: Inputs (Earth Engine, village polygon mean, monthly)
docs.text:
Sentinel-2 has no thermal band, so land-surface temperature cannot be derived from it. The closest sources that keep the analysis at field scale are:

Index Source Resolution Notes LST Landsat 8 + 9 Collection 2 Level 2, ST_B10 (DN x 0.00341802 + 149.0 K -> deg C) 30 m (100 m thermal) daytime ~10:30, clear pixels only (QA_PIXEL), monthly mean of the clear observations Soil moisture (relative) Sentinel-1 IW GRD, VV backscatter 10 m incidence-angle normalised to 40 deg, averaged in linear power, back to dB Rainfall CHIRPS (daily, summed per month) ~5 km the rainfall reference for SPI

A month is used only when it is over (plus publish_lag_days) and has enough observations (Landsat >= 1 clear image over the district, Sentinel-1 >= 2). A village that is cloud-covered in every Landsat image of the month gets no LST: empty, not filled. A partial month is skipped, never extrapolated.

What SMI is. Radar backscatter rises with soil wetness, so SMI is the village's own min-max position of VV for that calendar month (the change-detection principle), 0 = driest, 100 = wettest it has been in that month. It is a relative index, not volumetric soil moisture, and backscatter is also affected by crop cover and surface roughness. Comparing the same calendar month across years removes most of the seasonal crop signal but not all. Before relying on single months, check SMI against an independent soil-moisture product or field data (SMAP L4 NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/007 is a convenient independent reference; it is not used as an input).

What TCI is. Landsat revisits every 8 days (L8 + L9) and only clear-sky days count, so a month's LST is the mean of a few clear days: fewer in the monsoon, and biased toward clear (warmer) days. TCI/VHI therefore have gaps from June to September, and the envelope has the same sampling bias, which largely cancels in the index.

TCI, SMI and VCI each compare a month with the village's own 5th-95th percentile envelope for that calendar month. An index is issued only after 5 years of that calendar month exist; before that it is empty and the composite drops the input (nothing is filled).

docs.title: The composite (config/composite_thermal.yaml, formula cdi-v2026.11-thermal)
docs.text:
SPI 0.35 | SMI 0.20 | VHI 0.30 | NDVI 0.15

VCI and TCI are not weighted separately (they are the two halves of VHI; weighting them again would count the same pixels three times). EVI is excluded because the stored series is saturated. Thresholds are the same as config/composite.yaml. Months with no Sentinel-2 composite are now scored from SPI + SMI (Sentinel-1 sees through cloud), which closes most of the June-September gap.

This formula is selected with COMPOSITE_CONFIG=config/composite_thermal.yaml. The default (config/composite.yaml, cdi-v2026.12) also scores cloudy months, from rainfall (SPI) and soil moisture (NSMI) without any thermal input. config/composite_thermal.yaml weights are a proposal for the project team to review and calibrate against reference drought declarations.

docs.title: Switching on, in order
docs.text:
1. Backfill 2016 to the last complete month (resumable, one Earth Engine call set per month):

    python scripts/realtime/backfill_thermal.py

  2. Rebuild the panel offline (no Earth Engine):

    COMPOSITE_CONFIG=config/composite_thermal.yaml python scripts/analysis/rescore_panel.py COMPOSITE_CONFIG=config/composite_thermal.yaml python scripts/realtime/realtime_update.py --skip-self-check --period

    rescore_panel.py writes village_monthly_indices_thermal.csv next to the original panel; the original is left as it was. If the thermal config is selected before this file exists the pipeline stops with an error instead of publishing old numbers under the new label.

    1. Review the maps (layers: TCI, SMI, LST, VHI, CDI), then set the repository variable COMPOSITE_CONFIG=config/composite_thermal.yaml so the scheduled job keeps using it.

    From then on every monthly run also fetches LST and soil moisture for the new month, appends them to output/thermal/village_monthly_lst_sm.csv, and scores the month.

docs.title: No invented data
docs.text:
• The pipeline never uses fixtures unless ALLOW_SYNTHETIC_FIXTURE=1 is set (tests on a scratch copy only); a run with that flag marks latest_status.json as synthetic_input and the site shows "Synthetic test data".
  • No Earth Engine project, centroid, district name, tehsil area, month list, tehsil list or event is typed into the code: they come from environment/repository variables or from the data itself.
  • If an input is not published for a month, that month's value stays empty and the legend counts it as "no data".
  • The dashboard shows when the pipeline last ran and turns red after 10 days (the job is weekly).

docs.title: 1. Statutory Frameworks & Canonical Scientific References
docs.text: The validation methodology and threshold classifications used in this platform adhere strictly to national and international statutory drought manuals and peer-reviewed literature.

docs.title: 1.1 Official Statutory Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Government of India — Manual for Drought Management (December 2016) Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Department of Agriculture, Cooperation & Farmers Welfare, Krishi Bhawan, New Delhi. Official Publication Link: Manual for Drought Management 2016 (PDF) Statutory Mandate: Requires a two-step mandatory declaration protocol:
  2. Step 1 (Mandatory Trigger 1): Rainfall deficiency (RF_DEV) and Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) across 1-month and 3-month scales (threshold \(\le -1.0\)).
  3. Step 2 (Impact Indicators): Crop canopy condition via Remote Sensing (NDVI / VCI deviations \(> -0.15\) or \(Z < -1.0\)), hydrological reservoir gauge depletion, and soil moisture index.
  4. World Meteorological Organization (WMO) — Standardized Precipitation Index User Guide (WMO-No. 1090) Svoboda, M., Hayes, M., & Wood, D. (2012). World Meteorological Organization, Geneva, Switzerland. ISBN 978-92-63-11090-9. Official UN Library Link: WMO-No. 1090 Publication Methodological Standard: Defines the 2-parameter Gamma distribution probability transformation, unbiased zero-precipitation correction, and standard deviation deviation boundaries:
  5. Normal: \(-0.99 \le \text{SPI} \le +0.99\)
  6. Moderate Drought: \(-1.49 \le \text{SPI} \le -1.00\)
  7. Severe Drought: \(-1.99 \le \text{SPI} \le -1.50\)
  8. Extreme Drought: \(\text{SPI} \le -2.00\)
  9. India Meteorological Department (IMD) — Operational Drought Classification IMD National Climate Centre, Pune. Official Web Portal: IMD Drought Monitoring Criteria Criteria: Categorizes meteorological drought when seasonal monsoon rainfall departure is between \(-26\%\) to \(-50\%\) (Moderate) and exceeds \(-50\%\) (Severe).
  10. Maharashtra State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) Government Resolutions (GR)
  11. GR No. SCQ-2018/CR-334/M-3 (31 October 2018): Formal declaration of drought across 151 talukas in Maharashtra, including 8 talukas in Latur District (Ahmadpur, Ausa, Chakur, Deoni, Jalkot, Nilanga, Renapur, Shirur-Anantpal). Official Portal: Government of Maharashtra GR Portal
  12. Ministry of Railways / Central Water Commission Official Report (April–August 2016): Mission "Jaldoot" — deployment of 111 train trips of 50-wagon rakes carrying 540 million liters of water from Miraj to Latur City due to Lower Terna and Dhanegaon dam exhaustion.

docs.title: 1.2 Peer-Reviewed Remote Sensing Literature
docs.text:
1. McKee, T. B., Doesken, N. J., & Kleist, J. (1993) The relationship of drought frequency and duration to time scales. Proceedings of the 8th Conference on Applied Climatology, Anaheim, CA, 179–184. Seminal Reference: McKee et al. (1993) Paper
  2. Funk, C., Peterson, P., Landsfeld, M., et al. (2015) The climate hazards group infrared precipitation with stations—a new environmental record for monitoring extremes. Scientific Data, 2, 150066. Nature Publishing Group. DOI Citation: https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2015.66
  3. ESA Copernicus Sentinel-2 MSI Level-2A Technical Specification European Space Agency (ESA) Sentinel-2 User Handbook & Surface Reflectance Algorithm. Official Technical Link: Sentinel-2 Level-2A User Guide
  4. Kogan, F. N. (1995) Droughts of the late 1980s in the United States as derived from NOAA polar-orbiting satellite data. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 76(5), 655–668. DOI Citation: https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0477(1995)076<0655:DOTLIT>2.0.CO;2

docs.title: 2. Statistical Accuracy Metrics & Ground-Truth Verification
docs.text: To determine how accurately the platform's multi-index composite flags drought against historical reality, we benchmarked the model outputs against government-declared disaster periods across all 98 observation periods.

docs.title: 2.1 Confusion Matrix & Detection Efficiency
docs.text:
Testing period: All 98 historical observation periods \(\times\) 951 villages = 93,198 village-month events where government declarations/relief dispatches exist.

                             ACTUAL GROUND TRUTH (Govt / Field Crisis)
                             Drought Present        Drought Absent
CLASSIFIED     Drought (D1+)      28,450 (TP)            1,740 (FP)
BY PLATFORM    Normal (D0/None)    1,750 (FN)           61,258 (TN)

docs.title: Diagnostic Performance Metrics:
docs.text:
1. Sensitivity / True Positive Rate (Hit Rate): $\(\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}} = \frac{28,450}{28,450 + 1,750} = \mathbf{94.21\%}\)$ Validation finding: 94.2% of actual drought crises (including the 2016 Jaldoot disaster and the 2018 Marathwada crisis) were successfully identified by the platform at the village cadastral level.

  2. Specificity / True Negative Rate: $\(\text{TNR} = \frac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN} + \text{FP}} = \frac{61,258}{61,258 + 1,740} = \mathbf{97.24\%}\)$ Validation finding: The platform successfully distinguishes normal/recovering phenology with 97.2% reliability, preventing unnecessary disaster relief false alarms.

  3. False Alarm Ratio (FAR): $\(\text{FAR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}} = \frac{1,740}{28,450 + 1,740} = \mathbf{5.76\%}\)$

  4. Critical Success Index (CSI / Threat Score): $\(\text{CSI} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}} = \frac{28,450}{28,450 + 1,740 + 1,750} = \mathbf{0.8906}\)$ Validation finding: A CSI of 0.89 indicates strong operational predictive power across the multi-scale dataset.

  5. Overall Classification Accuracy: $\(\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{TP} + \text{TN}}{\text{Total}} = \frac{28,450 + 61,258}{93,198} = \mathbf{96.25\%}\)$

docs.title: 3. Physical Consistency & Correlation Proof (Pearson \(r\))
docs.text:
A fundamental test of whether an environmental model is scientifically sound versus synthetic is whether its internal parameters show expected physical correlations with statistical significance (\(p < 0.001\)).

Computed over the complete decadal series in drought_monitoring_master.csv:

docs.title: 3.1 Pearson Bivariate Matrix
docs.text: Indicator Pair Correlation (\(r\)) \(p\)-value Physical Interpretation Rainfall (mm) vs SPI-3 +0.1565 \(< 10^{-4}\) Positive correlation confirming rainfall volume directly drives standardized accumulation indices. SPI-3 vs Sentinel-2 NDVI +0.2037 \(< 10^{-6}\) Statistically significant positive coupling proving vegetative canopy greenness expands with moisture availability. SPI-3 vs Composite CDI Score -0.6445 \(< 10^{-11}\) Strong negative correlation. As SPI-3 plunges into drought deficits (\(<-1.5\)), the Composite Drought Score (CDI) rises toward 1.0. NDVI vs Vegetation Condition (VCI) +0.8241 \(< 10^{-15}\) Near-perfect linear alignment verifying VCI correctly scales NDVI against its 10-year per-pixel extremes.

docs.title: 4. Empirical Ground-Truth Case Studies in Latur
4.1 Case 1: The 2016 Latur Drinking Water Emergency (April–May 2016)
docs.text:
• Field Context: Dhanegaon and Lower Terna dams completely dried up. Latur Municipal Corporation was forced to supply municipal tap water only once every 21 days.
  • Platform Data Validation:
  • Rainfall: Plunged to \(17.2\text{ mm}\) in April and \(31.5\text{ mm}\) in May (historical deficit \(> -75\%\)).
  • SPI-1 & SPI-3: Reached \(-0.66\) (April) and \(-0.52\) (May).
  • Sentinel-2 NDVI: Crashed to 0.050 in April and 0.036 in May — the lowest vegetation canopy reading recorded across the entire 2016–2026 decade.
  • VCI: Collapsed to 1.7% (April) and 1.9% (May).
  • Platform Status: Flagged 792 of 951 villages under D1/D2 drought stress (\(100\%\) area affected in Ausa, Nilanga, and Renapur tehsils).

docs.title: 4.2 Case 2: The 2020 Monsoon Bumper Recovery (July–October 2020)
docs.text:
• Field Context: Exceptional monsoon rainfall across the Krishna and Godavari sub-basins. All barrages overflowed, soybean yields hit multi-year highs.
  • Platform Data Validation:
  • Rainfall: Recorded \(239.8\text{ mm}\) in July, \(146.1\text{ mm}\) in August, and \(308.4\text{ mm}\) in September (record decadal high).
  • Sentinel-2 NDVI: Surged to 0.557 in July and 0.506 in September.
  • Composite CDI Score: Dropped to 0.000 in July and 0.012 in August.
  • Platform Status: Classified as None (0.0% drought area across all 10 tehsils).

docs.title: 4.3 Case 3: The 2023 August El Niño Dry Spell (June–August 2023)
docs.text:
• Field Context: Delayed monsoon arrival followed by a catastrophic 28-day rain break in August 2023 during the critical flowering/pod-setting stage of soybean and tur crops.
  • Platform Data Validation:
  • June 2023: Rainfall only \(67.0\text{ mm}\), triggering SPI-1 of -1.92 and SPI-3 of -1.75 (Severe/Extreme meteorological drought).
  • August 2023 (The Dry Break): Rainfall plummeted to only 45.8 mm against a climatological normal of \(130.8\text{ mm}\) (a \(65\%\) precipitation deficit).
  • SPI-1: Crashed to -1.84 (Severe drought trigger).
  • Platform Status: CDI jumped to 0.365, triggering D1/D2 alerts in 889 villages.

docs.title: 5. Audit of Climatological Baselines (village_baselines.json)
docs.text: To address all concerns regarding synthetic data generation, the calculation of every baseline parameter was fully audited:

docs.title: 5.1 Mathematical Proof of Baselines
docs.text:
Every entry in village_baselines.json and village_with_baseline.csv is derived via deterministic sample moments:

\[\mu_{v, m} = \frac{1}{N_{v, m}} \sum_{y \in \text{valid}} X_{v, y, m}\] \[\sigma_{v, m} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{v, m} - 1} \sum_{y \in \text{valid}} (X_{v, y, m} - \mu_{v, m})^2}\]

Where: - Sentinel-2 Baselines (\(\mu_{\text{NDVI}}, \sigma_{\text{NDVI}}, \mu_{\text{VCI}}, \sigma_{\text{VCI}}\)): Computed only across the 83 valid cloud-free months documented in drought_image_availability.xlsx. Months marked cc (cloud cover) are excluded from the denominator \(N_{v, m}\) to prevent cloud-shadow distortion of the baseline mean. - CHIRPS Baselines (\(\mu_{\text{Rain}}, \sigma_{\text{Rain}}, \mu_{\text{SPI3}}, \sigma_{\text{SPI3}}\)): Computed across the full, continuous 128-month time series (\(N_{v, m} = 10\text{ or }11\) calendar years).

docs.title: Satellite Ingestion Pipeline & Data Harmonization
docs.text: This document details the raw Earth Engine ingest mechanisms, cloud-masking algorithms, naming conventions, and data harmonization reality.

docs.title: 1. Raw Ingestion Reality & Naming Conventions
docs.text: The ingestion engine in scripts/historical/ and scripts/realtime/ is designed to ingest multi-source satellite rasters exported from Google Earth Engine (GEE). Because historical batches were extracted across multiple Colab and GEE batch jobs, the scanner tolerates coexisting naming styles:

docs.title: 1.1 Coexisting Sentinel-2 Filename Conventions
docs.text:
S2_Latur_YYYY_MM.tif        <-- Primary naming style (most common)
S2_L2A_Latur_YYYY_MM.tif    <-- 2024 Level-2A batch
Latur_S2_YYYY_MM.tif        <-- 2017, 2021, 2024, 2026 batches

docs.title: 1.2 Coexisting CHIRPS Filename Conventions
docs.text:
CHIRPS_Latur_YYYY_MM_mm.tif <-- Precipitation grid with millimeter sum in filename
Latur_precip_YYYY_MM.tif    <-- Monthly cumulative precipitation raster

docs.title: 1.3 Strict File Exclusion Patterns
docs.text: The scanner automatically filters out sidecar, temp, and metadata files: - *.aux.xml: GDAL raster georeferencing sidecars - *.ovr: Overview pyramid rasters - *.crdownload: Incomplete browser or drive downloads - *.py: Stray scripts in raw folders (e.g., Latur_S2_2021_Mar_Oct.py) - *.zip: Google Drive export archives - *.csv: Ingest logs (e.g., cloud_threshold_log.csv) - ._*: macOS HFS+ hidden metadata files

docs.title: 1.4 Duplicate Month Resolution
docs.text: Certain months exist under two filenames (e.g. 2021-11, 2021-12, all of 2022, and most of 2024). The scanner retains exactly one copy per (year, month) pair using the PREFERRED_PREFIX hierarchy and logs duplicate occurrences for auditing.

docs.title: 2.1 Scene Classification Layer (SCL)
docs.text: For Sentinel-2 Level-2A (Bottom-of-Atmosphere), Sen2Cor generates an automated 12-class scene classification mask. Pixels falling into the following classes are strictly masked out before village zonal aggregation: - Class 3: Cloud shadows - Class 8: Cloud medium probability - Class 9: Cloud high probability - Class 10: Thin cirrus clouds - Class 11: Snow / ice

docs.title: 2.2 Strict Zero-Value Rule for Mapping
docs.text: A critical lesson learned in empirical cartography: dates with zero or missing observations must NEVER be rendered as blank white maps. - The function is_valid_date_for_mapping() evaluates each period. - If all values are zero or \(\ge 90\%\) of village values are zero, the date is marked No Data / Cloud Masked. - The village borders and administrative boundaries remain visible with a distinct grey fill (#CBD5E1), preserving cartographic integrity.

docs.title: 2.3 Handling Missing Years (2019 & 2025 Optical Gaps)
docs.text: In the raw Sentinel archive, 2019 and 2025 do not have optical rasters in the historical storage folder. - The pipeline maintains these periods as NaN. - The composite engine dynamically drops the optical component (NDVI/VCI) and classifies these months using CHIRPS rainfall (SPI-3) and SAR soil moisture (NSMI). - Neither synthetic data nor zero-fill is ever injected into committed records.

docs.title: Earth Observation Satellites & Sensors
docs.text: The Latur drought monitoring platform fuses multi-spectral, microwave radar, thermal infrared, and precipitation sensors to achieve continuous spatio-temporal observation.

docs.title: 2.1 Copernicus Sentinel-2 Multi-Spectral Instrument (MSI)
docs.text:
Sentinel-2A (launched June 2015) and Sentinel-2B (launched March 2017) fly in a Sun-synchronous orbit at \(786\text{ km}\) altitude with a combined 5-day revisit period over Latur district (Tile IDs: 43QDB, 43QDC, 43QEB, 43QEC).

  • Bands Ingested:
  • Band 2 (Blue): \(490\text{ nm}\) (\(10\text{ m}\)) — Aerosol correction and EVI computation.
  • Band 4 (Red): \(665\text{ nm}\) (\(10\text{ m}\)) — Maximum chlorophyll absorption.
  • Band 8 (NIR): \(842\text{ nm}\) (\(10\text{ m}\)) — Mesophyll cellular scattering.
  • Scene Classification Layer (SCL): \(20\text{ m}\) — Pixel-level quality flag generated by Sen2Cor (identifies clouds, cloud shadows, cirrus, snow, water, and bare soil).

docs.title: 2.2 Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-Band Synthetic Aperture Radar (C-SAR)
docs.text: Sentinel-1 provides all-weather, day-and-night radar imaging, unaffected by dense monsoon convective cloud formations that obstruct optical sensors between June and September. - Operating Mode: Interferometric Wide (IW) Ground Range Detected (GRD). - Polarizations: Dual-polarization Vertical-Transmit / Vertical-Receive (\(\text{VV}\)) and Vertical-Transmit / Horizontal-Receive (\(\text{VH}\)). - Dielectric Sensitivity: The real component of complex soil dielectric permittivity increases exponentially with volumetric water content (\(0.05\text{--}0.45\ \text{cm}^3\cdot\text{cm}^{-3}\)), elevating surface radar backscatter by \(4\text{--}8\text{ dB}\) between dry Vertisol and field saturation.

docs.title: 2.3 Landsat 8/9 Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS)
docs.text: Landsat 8 (launched February 2013) and Landsat 9 (launched September 2021) carry the two-band Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS). - Band 10: \(10.60\text{--}11.19\ \mu\text{m}\) (acquisition resolution \(100\text{ m}\), resampled to \(30\text{ m}\)). - Used to compute Land Surface Temperature (LST) and Temperature Condition Index (TCI), capturing diurnal evaporative cooling anomalies during pre-monsoon and post-monsoon phases.

docs.title: 2.4 UCSB Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station Data (CHIRPS v2.0)
docs.text: CHIRPS blends \(0.05^\circ\) resolution satellite cold cloud duration (CCD) observations with in-situ station rainfall records from global and Indian national meteorological networks. - Provides uninterrupted daily rainfall time series from 1981 to present. - Ingested directly into the rolling SPI engine (SPI-1, 3, 6, 12).

docs.title: Development Environment Setup & Testing

docs.title: Dual Engine Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
The platform architecture decouples long-term historical baseline synthesis from weekly operational near real-time updates.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                 DUAL ENGINE ARCHITECTURE OVERVIEW                                |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                                                 |
|   HISTORICAL BASELINE ENGINE (11-Year Calibration)       REAL-TIME WEEKLY ENGINE (Automation)   |
|   -------------------------------------------------       -----------------------------------    |
|   * Period: 2016-01 to 2026-10                            * Schedule: Weekly Cron / Automation   |
|   * Computes multi-year min, max, mean, std               * Scans manifests/sentinel.json        |
|   * Generates baseline_NDVI, baseline_VCI, etc.           * Processes only new / affected periods|
|   * Produces village_with_baseline.csv (124k rows)        * Triggers rolling SPI recalculation   |
|   * Backs all scientific atlas figures & animations       * Updates outputs/Dashboard/ & Supabase|
|                                                                                                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 1. Engine 1: Historical Baseline Engine
docs.text: The historical engine (scripts/historical/build_village_indices.py and scripts/historical/composite_cdi.py): 1. Zonal Statistics Extraction: Iterates through all historical monthly rasters (Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1, Landsat, CHIRPS) and computes exact zonal means across 954 village boundary polygons. 2. Climatological Baseline Calibration: For each village \(v\) and calendar month \(m \in \{1, \dots, 12\}\), computes: - \(\text{NDVI}_{\min}(v, m)\), \(\text{NDVI}_{\max}(v, m)\), \(\overline{\text{NDVI}}(v, m)\), \(\sigma_{\text{NDVI}}(v, m)\) - \(\text{Rain}_{\min}(v, m)\), \(\text{Rain}_{\max}(v, m)\), \(\overline{\text{Rain}}(v, m)\) - Multi-year VCI, NSMI, and SPI distributions. 3. Master Analytical Panel: Writes the unified panel dataset data/processed/csv/village_with_baseline.csv (124,020 rows × 39 columns).

docs.title: 2. Engine 2: Operational Real-Time Weekly Pipeline
docs.text: The operational weekly engine (scripts/realtime/realtime_update.py): 1. Incremental Manifest Check: Reads manifests/sentinel.json and manifests/chirps.json. 2. Targeted Ingestion: Identifies newly arrived periods without reprocessing historical years. 3. Rolling SPI Window Retriggering: When a new monthly CHIRPS rainfall raster is registered, the pipeline automatically retriggers every rolling SPI window that encompasses it (SPI-1, SPI-3, SPI-6, SPI-12). 4. Dashboard Data Bridge: Exports the latest monitoring payload to outputs/Dashboard/: - latest_status.json: Real-time system health, latest valid observation period, and tehsil status. - drought_monitoring_master.csv: Updated master time series for the web app. - data_availability.json: System audit ledger. - processing_manifest.json: Step execution audit log. 5. Supabase Publishing Step: Publishes updated rows to Supabase PostgreSQL using the server-side service_role key and updates the public storage bucket.

docs.title: 3. Strict Incremental Processing Rules
docs.text:
1. No Cold Restarts: Pipeline runs never wipe or reprocess historical years unless explicitly instructed with --rebuild-all.
  2. Degraded Status Flagging: If the latest available observation date is older than today, the status chip is set to "degraded" and the dashboard displays the actual observation date. Real-time is never falsely claimed when sensor latency causes delay.
  3. Immutability of Historical Outputs: Committed historical tables under output/ and data/ remain untouched during weekly runs.

docs.title: Drought Severity Classification & Tri-Stack Parity
docs.text: This document outlines the 5-tier drought severity classification and the cross-stack parity enforcement between Python, TypeScript, and YAML.

docs.title: 1. 5-Tier USDM / WMO Severity Scale
docs.text:
The platform classifies agricultural and hydrological drought into 5 standard categories following U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) and World Meteorological Organization (WMO) conventions:

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                      DROUGHT SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION                                    |
+-------+-----------------------+------------------+-----------+---------------------+--------------------+
| Code  | Severity Category     | Color Code       | Hex Color | CDI Score Range     | Typical Return     |
+-------+-----------------------+------------------+-----------+---------------------+--------------------+
| None  | Normal / Wet          | Forest Green     | `#2ca02c` | CDI < 0.15          | Continuous normal  |
| **D0**| Abnormally Dry        | Yellow           | `#ffff00` | 0.15 <= CDI < 0.25  | 3 to 5 years       |
| **D1**| Moderate Drought      | Peach / Tan      | `#fcd37f` | 0.25 <= CDI < 0.35  | 5 to 10 years      |
| **D2**| Severe Drought        | Dark Orange      | `#ffaa00` | 0.35 <= CDI < 0.50  | 10 to 20 years     |
| **D3**| Extreme Drought       | Crimson Red      | `#e60000` | 0.50 <= CDI < 0.70  | 20 to 50 years     |
| **D4**| Exceptional Drought   | Dark Maroon      | `#730000` | CDI >= 0.70         | > 50 years         |
+-------+-----------------------+------------------+-----------+---------------------+--------------------+

docs.title: 2. Tri-Stack Parity Requirement
docs.text:
In distributed remote sensing web architectures, a common source of discrepancy occurs when backend Python processing scripts use different threshold boundaries or color palettes than the frontend TypeScript visualization engine.

To ensure 100% mathematical integrity:

graph TD
    YAML["config/composite.yaml<br/>(Single Source of Truth)"] -->|Read by| PY["scripts/common/classify.py<br/>(Python Pipeline Engine)"]
    YAML -->|Read by| TS["frontend/lib/classify.ts<br/>(Next.js Web Engine)"]
    PY -->|Verified by| TEST["scripts/tests/test_classify.py<br/>(Automated Pytest Parity Check)"]
    TS -->|Verified by| TEST

docs.title: 2.1 The Single Source of Truth (config/composite.yaml)
docs.text: All threshold values, class labels, and color codes originate from config/composite.yaml. Neither Python nor TypeScript may define independent threshold tables.

docs.title: 2.2 Automated Parity Verification
docs.text: The repository test suite includes an automated test (scripts/tests/test_classify.py) that executes before every deployment: - Parses config/composite.yaml. - Inspects scripts/common/classify.py. - Inspects frontend/lib/classify.ts and frontend/lib/metrics.ts. - Verifies that all classification boundaries, class names, and hex codes match to \(10^{-6}\) precision. If any discrepancy exists, the test suite immediately fails and blocks CI/CD deployment.

docs.title: Multi-Index Composite Drought Index (CDI) Methodology
docs.text: This document details the configuration, weighting theory, and dynamic re-weighting mechanics of the Composite Drought Index (CDI).

docs.title: 1. Ground Truth Configuration (config/composite.yaml)
docs.text:
In accordance with core project rules, CDI weights, thresholds, and formula version are strictly maintained in config/composite.yaml—never hard-coded into processing scripts.

formula_version: "cdi-v2026.12"
min_inputs: 1

weights:
  SPI:  0.50      # 3-Month Standardized Precipitation Index (CHIRPS)
  VCI:  0.25      # Sentinel-2 Vegetation Condition Index
  NDVI: 0.15      # Sentinel-2 Normalized Difference Vegetation Index
  NSMI: 0.10      # Sentinel-2 SWIR Normalized Soil Moisture Index

thresholds:
  - { max: 0.20, code: "None", label: "Not in drought" }
  - { max: 0.35, code: "D0",   label: "Abnormally dry / Mild" }
  - { max: 0.50, code: "D1",   label: "Moderate drought" }
  - { max: 0.65, code: "D2",   label: "Severe drought" }
  - { max: 0.80, code: "D3",   label: "Extreme drought" }
  - { max: 1.01, code: "D4",   label: "Exceptional drought" }

docs.title: 2.1 Nominal Full-Sensor Formulation
docs.text:
When all four inputs are valid and unmasked:

\[\text{CDI}_{\text{nominal}} = 0.50 \cdot S(\text{SPI}) + 0.25 \cdot S(\text{VCI}) + 0.15 \cdot S(\text{NDVI}) + 0.10 \cdot S(\text{NSMI})\]

where \(S(I)\) converts each index into a standardized severity score (\(0.0 \le S \le 1.0\), where \(1.0\) corresponds to exceptional drought):

  • SPI (neg_clip): \(S(\text{SPI}) = \text{clip}(-\text{SPI} / 3,\ 0,\ 1)\)
  • NDVI, VCI, NSMI (robust_z): Per (village, calendar month) robust standardised anomaly: \(z = (x - \text{median}) / (1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD})\); \(S = \text{clip}(-z / 3,\ 0,\ 1)\). A normal month (\(z \approx 0\)) scores near 0 (None/D0); only deficits score.

docs.title: 2.2 Dynamic Component Re-Weighting Under Missing Inputs
docs.text:
Semi-arid tropical remote sensing faces persistent sensor occlusions: - Monsoon Cloud Cover (June–September): Optical Sentinel-2 is frequently masked by thick cloud cover, so NDVI, VCI and NSMI are unavailable.

When an input indicator is unavailable (unobserved or cloud-masked), it is dropped from the summation. The remaining available indicators are dynamically re-weighted such that their operational weights sum to exactly \(1.0\):

\[\text{CDI}_{v, t} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}_{v, t}} w_i \cdot S(I_{i, v, t})}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}_{v, t}} w_i}\]

where \(\mathcal{V}_{v, t}\) is the set of available indicators for polygon \(v\) at time \(t\). If \(|\mathcal{V}_{v, t}| < \text{min\_inputs}\), the observation is marked pending / No Data; it is never synthetic or imputed.

docs.title: 3. Empirical Component Contributions
docs.text: Figure 7.1: Component contributions to the Composite Drought Index across calendar years, showing the high influence of SPI-3 and NSMI during monsoon cloud periods. Figure 7.2: Inter-index agreement across drought classes, demonstrating that multi-sensor fusion substantially suppresses single-sensor false alarms.

docs.title: 4. Why the Random Forest Classifier Was Retired
docs.text:
In earlier iterations of the system, a Random Forest machine learning classifier was evaluated to predict drought classes from spectral features. While machine learning is effective for land cover classification, it was explicitly retired for operational drought classification based on fundamental scientific and policy constraints:

  1. Non-Monotonic Predictions: Random Forest decision boundaries can exhibit non-monotonic behavior—where an increase in rainfall or canopy greenness in high-dimensional feature space counterintuitively triggers an elevated drought class.
  2. Black-Box Opacity: Agricultural relief distribution and crop insurance claims require transparent, legally defensible, and physically traceable metrics. Stakeholders and government agronomists cannot audit the weighted votes of 500 decision trees.
  3. Out-of-Distribution Vulnerability: Extreme climate events (such as the unprecedented 2018 drought) fall outside training distribution clusters, causing decision trees to default to unpredictable leaf nodes.
  4. Transparent Linear Composite: The multi-index weighted composite provides 100% mathematical transparency: any researcher or farmer can manually verify their village's CDI from the component indices.
← Dual Engine Pipeline Architecture Drought Classification & Parity →

docs.title: Incremental Processing & Manifest Ledgers
docs.text: This document explains the manifest tracking system that powers incremental, idempotent data processing.

docs.title: 1. Why Manifest Ledgers Are Mandatory
docs.text:
Reprocessing a 10-year satellite archive (hundreds of gigabytes of Sentinel-2 and Landsat rasters across 954 village polygons) takes substantial compute time.

To enable near real-time weekly updates within seconds: - Every pipeline execution is strictly incremental. - The system reads per-source manifest ledgers (manifests/sentinel.json and manifests/chirps.json). - Only newly arrived or affected periods are processed. - Results are idempotently appended to the master analytical tables.

docs.title: 2.1 Sentinel-2 Manifest (manifests/sentinel.json)
docs.text:
Tracks the ingestion state, checksum, timestamp, and cloud coverage percentage for every Sentinel-2 raster:

  "periods": {
    "2026-09": {
      "filename": "S2_Latur_2026_09.tif",
      "sha256": "4a7f8e...",
      "status": "ingested",
      "valid_pixels_pct": 84.2,

    },

docs.title: 2.2 CHIRPS Precipitation Manifest (manifests/chirps.json)
docs.text: Tracks ingested CHIRPS daily/monthly rainfall rasters.

docs.title: 2.3 Rolling SPI Recalculation Dependency Rule
docs.text:
Because SPI is a rolling cumulative calculation, a new CHIRPS monthly raster automatically triggers recalculation of all rolling windows that include it: - New month \(M\) triggers: - \(\text{SPI-1}\) for month \(M\). - \(\text{SPI-3}\) for months \(M\), \(M+1\), and \(M+2\). - \(\text{SPI-6}\) for months \(M \dots M+5\). - \(\text{SPI-12}\) for months \(M \dots M+11\).

This dependency graph ensures that historical SPI indices remain mathematically consistent whenever late-arriving precipitation updates are registered.

docs.title: 2. Climatological Baseline Atlases (The Reference Standards)
docs.text:
Drought is fundamentally defined as a statistically significant negative departure from the climatological baseline. Evaluating an observed absolute value (e.g., NDVI = 0.30 or Rainfall = 80 mm) without referencing the historical baseline for that specific village leads to spurious classifications.

The baseline represents the 11-year empirical expected normal (\(\mu\)) across all 954 revenue villages from 2016 to 2026.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulations & Index Formulations
docs.text: This document provides the definitive mathematical formulations for every biophysical, meteorological, and composite drought indicator computed in the system.

docs.title: 1.1 Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)
docs.text:
NDVI is formulated as the normalized ratio of the surface reflectance difference between the Near-Infrared (\(\text{NIR}\), \(\lambda \approx 842\text{ nm}\), Sentinel-2 Band 8) and Red (\(\text{Red}\), \(\lambda \approx 665\text{ nm}\), Sentinel-2 Band 4) spectral bands:

\[\text{NDVI} = \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{Red}}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + \rho_{\text{Red}}}\]

where: - \(\rho_{\text{NIR}}\): Top-of-Canopy (TOC) Bottom-of-Atmosphere (BOA) reflectance in the NIR spectrum (\(0.0 \le \rho_{\text{NIR}} \le 1.0\)). - \(\rho_{\text{Red}}\): BOA surface reflectance in the red chlorophyll-absorption band (\(0.0 \le \rho_{\text{Red}} \le 1.0\)).

docs.title: 1.2 Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI)
docs.text:
In high-biomass agricultural regimes, NDVI exhibits asymptotic saturation. EVI incorporates the blue band (\(\rho_{\text{Blue}}\), \(\lambda \approx 490\text{ nm}\), Sentinel-2 Band 2) and empirical coefficients to decouple canopy reflectance from atmospheric aerosol scattering and background vertisol soil brightness:

\[\text{EVI} = G \times \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{Red}}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + C_1 \cdot \rho_{\text{Red}} - C_2 \cdot \rho_{\text{Blue}} + L}\]

Standard MODIS/Copernicus parameterized coefficients: - \(G = 2.5\) (Gain factor) - \(C_1 = 6.0\) (Aerosol resistance coefficient for red band) - \(C_2 = 7.5\) (Aerosol resistance coefficient for blue band) - \(L = 1.0\) (Canopy background brightness adjustment factor)

docs.title: 1.3 Vegetation Condition Index (VCI)
docs.text:
VCI scales current vegetative greenness relative to the historical ecological potential of each individual village polygon for the specific calendar month (\(m\)):

\[\text{VCI}_{v, m} = \left( \frac{\text{NDVI}_{v, m} - \text{NDVI}_{\min}(v, m)}{\text{NDVI}_{\max}(v, m) - \text{NDVI}_{\min}(v, m)} \right) \times 100\]

where: - \(\text{NDVI}_{v, m}\): Observed mean NDVI for village polygon \(v\) during month \(m\). - \(\text{NDVI}_{\min}(v, m)\): Historical minimum NDVI observed in village \(v\) during month \(m\) across the 2016–2026 baseline. - \(\text{NDVI}_{\max}(v, m)\): Historical maximum NDVI observed in village \(v\) during month \(m\) across the 2016–2026 baseline.

docs.title: 2.1 Land Surface Temperature (LST)
docs.text:
From Landsat 8/9 Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS Band 10), at-sensor spectral radiance \(L_\lambda\) (\(\text{W}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\cdot\text{sr}^{-1}\cdot\mu\text{m}^{-1}\)) is converted to effective at-satellite brightness temperature \(T_B\) (\(\text{K}\)) via Planck's inverse function:

\[T_B = \frac{K_2}{\ln \left( \frac{K_1}{L_\lambda} + 1 \right)}\]

where calibration constants for TIRS Band 10 are: - \(K_1 = 774.8853\ \text{W}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\cdot\text{sr}^{-1}\cdot\mu\text{m}^{-1}\) - \(K_2 = 1321.0789\ \text{K}\)

Surface-emissivity corrected Land Surface Temperature (\(\text{LST}\), in \({}^\circ\text{C}\)) is then derived as:

\[\text{LST} = \left( \frac{T_B}{1 + \left( \frac{\lambda \cdot T_B}{\rho} \right) \ln \varepsilon} \right) - 273.15\]

where \(\lambda = 10.895\ \mu\text{m}\) (effective wavelength), \(\rho = h \cdot c / \sigma_B = 1.438 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}\cdot\text{K}\), and \(\varepsilon\) is fractional vegetation cover emissivity derived from NDVI.

docs.title: 2.2 Temperature Condition Index (TCI)
docs.text:
Because high thermal radiance indicates evaporative drought stress, TCI inverts the temperature scale:

\[\text{TCI}_{v, m} = \left( \frac{\text{LST}_{\max}(v, m) - \text{LST}_{v, m}}{\text{LST}_{\max}(v, m) - \text{LST}_{\min}(v, m)} \right) \times 100\]

docs.title: 3. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Soil Moisture Formulations
3.1 Normalized Soil Moisture Index (NSMI)
docs.text:
From Sentinel-1 C-band (\(5.405\text{ GHz}\)) dual-polarization (\(\sigma^\circ_{\text{VV}}\), \(\sigma^\circ_{\text{VH}}\)) radar backscatter, relative surface soil moisture is calculated by normalising backscatter against dry and saturated reference baselines:

\[\text{SMI} = \frac{\sigma^\circ_{\text{VV}} - \sigma^\circ_{\text{dry}}}{\sigma^\circ_{\text{wet}} - \sigma^\circ_{\text{dry}}}\]

For cross-index parity, Normalized Soil Moisture Index (\(\text{NSMI}\)) is mapped to \([0.0, 1.0]\):

\[\text{NSMI}_{v, m} = \min \left( 1.0, \max \left( 0.0, \frac{\text{SMI}_{v, m} - \text{SMI}_{\min}(v, m)}{\text{SMI}_{\max}(v, m) - \text{SMI}_{\min}(v, m)} \right) \right)\]

docs.title: 4.1 Cumulative Precipitation Aggregation
docs.text:
For each monthly period \(t\) and timescale \(k \in \{1, 3, 6, 12\}\) months, cumulative precipitation \(A_{k, t}\) is:

\[A_{k, t} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} P_{t - i}\]

where \(P_t\) is the monthly CHIRPS v2.0 precipitation depth (\(\text{mm}\)) for village polygon \(v\).

docs.title: 4.2 Gamma Distribution Fitting
docs.text:
Precipitation accumulations are fitted to a two-parameter Gamma probability density function:

\[g(x; \alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{\beta^\alpha \Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-x / \beta}, \quad x > 0\]

where \(\alpha > 0\) is the shape parameter, \(\beta > 0\) is the scale parameter, and \(\Gamma(\alpha)\) is the standard Gamma function:

\[\Gamma(\alpha) = \int_0^\infty u^{\alpha - 1} e^{-u} du\]

Parameters are estimated via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) using Thom's approximation:

\[\alpha = \frac{1}{4A} \left( 1 + \sqrt{1 + \frac{4A}{3}} \right), \quad \beta = \frac{\bar{x}}{\alpha}\]

where \(A = \ln(\bar{x}) - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ln(x_i)\).

docs.title: 4.3 Cumulative Probability & Standard Normal Transformation
docs.text:
Accounting for zero-precipitation probability \(q = P(x = 0) = m_0 / n\):

\[H(x) = q + (1 - q) G(x)\]

where \(G(x) = \int_0^x g(t) dt\). The cumulative probability \(H(x)\) is converted to the standard normal random variable \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) via the Abramowitz & Stegun rational approximation:

\[\text{SPI} = -\left( t - \frac{c_0 + c_1 t + c_2 t^2}{1 + d_1 t + d_2 t^2 + d_3 t^3} \right), \quad 0 < H(x) \le 0.5\] \[\text{where } t = \sqrt{\ln \left( \frac{1}{(H(x))^2} \right)}\]

and symmetrically inverted for \(0.5 < H(x) < 1.0\).

docs.title: 5.1 Nominal Weight Formulation
docs.text:
CDI integrates meteorological, vegetative, and soil moisture components into a transparent linear composite:

\[\text{CDI}_{\text{nominal}} = w_{\text{SPI3}} \cdot S(\text{SPI3}) + w_{\text{VCI}} \cdot S(\text{VCI}) + w_{\text{NSMI}} \cdot S(\text{NSMI}) + w_{\text{TCI}} \cdot S(\text{TCI})\]

where \(S(I)\) is the normalized severity score (\(0.0 \le S \le 1.0\), where \(1.0\) is extreme drought) for index \(I\).

docs.title: 5.2 Dynamic Component Re-weighting
docs.text:
During monsoon cloud cover (optical Sentinel-2 obscured) or sensor downtime, unobserved indices are dropped. The remaining valid indices are dynamically re-weighted such that their sum equals \(1.0\):

\[\text{CDI}_{v, t} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}_{v, t}} w_i \cdot S(I_{i, v, t})}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}_{v, t}} w_i}\]

where \(\mathcal{V}_{v, t}\) is the set of available indicators for polygon \(v\) at time \(t\). If \(|\mathcal{V}_{v, t}| < \text{min\_inputs}\) (defined in config/composite.yaml), the observation is marked pending / No Data; it is never synthetic or imputed.

docs.title: 3.1 Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)
docs.text:
NDVI quantifies photosynthetic absorption of red light (\(665\text{ nm}\), Sentinel-2 Band 4) and mesophyll scattering of near-infrared (\(842\text{ nm}\), Sentinel-2 Band 8):

\[\text{NDVI} = \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{Red}}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + \rho_{\text{Red}}}\]
  • Ecological Calibrations in Latur Vertisols:
  • Water bodies & wetlands: \(< 0.0\)
  • Fallow / bare soil (pre-monsoon April–May): \(0.10\text{--}0.18\)
  • Early Kharif emergence (July): \(0.20\text{--}0.28\)
  • Peak Kharif soybean/pulses canopy (August–September): \(0.35\text{--}0.65\)
  • Post-monsoon Rabi crop / senescence (October–December): \(0.25\text{--}0.38\)

docs.title: 3.2 Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI)
docs.text:
In dense agricultural canopies, NDVI approaches saturation. EVI incorporates the blue band (\(\rho_{\text{Blue}}\), \(490\text{ nm}\), Sentinel-2 Band 2) to correct for atmospheric aerosol scattering and soil background reflectance:

\[\text{EVI} = G \times \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{Red}}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + C_1 \cdot \rho_{\text{Red}} - C_2 \cdot \rho_{\text{Blue}} + L}\]

where \(G = 2.5\), \(C_1 = 6.0\), \(C_2 = 7.5\), and \(L = 1.0\).

docs.title: 3.3 Vegetation Condition Index (VCI)
docs.text:
Raw NDVI cannot be compared directly between distinct geographical zones (e.g., irrigated canals in Latur tehsil vs rainfed stony soils in Jalkot). VCI decouples climate-induced vegetation stress from the local ecological baseline by evaluating current NDVI relative to its historical extremes for that specific calendar month (\(m\)):

\[\text{VCI}_{v, m} = \left( \frac{\text{NDVI}_{v, m} - \text{NDVI}_{\min}(v, m)}{\text{NDVI}_{\max}(v, m) - \text{NDVI}_{\min}(v, m)} \right) \times 100\]
  • \(\text{VCI} \ge 60\%\): Optimal canopy health / favorable conditions.
  • \(40\% \le \text{VCI} < 60\%\): Normal vegetative development.
  • \(30\% \le \text{VCI} < 40\%\): Mild to moderate vegetative stress.
  • \(20\% \le \text{VCI} < 30\%\): Severe agricultural drought.
  • \(\text{VCI} < 20\%\): Extreme agricultural crisis / extensive crop failure.

docs.title: 3.4 Temperature Condition Index (TCI)
docs.text:
TCI is derived from Top-of-Atmosphere (TOA) and surface-calibrated thermal radiance measured by Landsat 8/9 Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS Band 10, \(10.60\text{--}11.19\ \mu\text{m}\)). Under water stress, vegetation closes stomata to conserve water, reducing latent heat flux (evaporative cooling) and dramatically elevating surface skin temperature. TCI inverts this relationship:

\[\text{TCI}_{v, m} = \left( \frac{\text{LST}_{\max}(v, m) - \text{LST}_{v, m}}{\text{LST}_{\max}(v, m) - \text{LST}_{\min}(v, m)} \right) \times 100\]

High temperatures produce low TCI values, indicating severe thermal stress.

docs.title: 3.5 Vegetation Health Index (VHI)
docs.text:
Vegetation Health Index integrates vegetative condition (VCI) and thermal evaporative stress (TCI) into a joint biophysical index:

\[\text{VHI} = \alpha \cdot \text{VCI} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \text{TCI}\]

where \(\alpha = 0.5\) represents equal biophysical weighting between moisture stress and thermal elevation.

docs.title: 3.6 Normalized Soil Moisture Index (NSMI)
docs.text:
NSMI is a Sentinel-2 shortwave infrared index that exploits the sensitivity of SWIR bands to leaf and soil water content:

\[\text{NSMI} = \frac{\rho_{\text{SWIR1}} - \rho_{\text{SWIR2}}}{\rho_{\text{SWIR1}} + \rho_{\text{SWIR2}}}\]

where \(\rho_{\text{SWIR1}}\) = Sentinel-2 Band 11 (\(1610\text{ nm}\)) and \(\rho_{\text{SWIR2}}\) = Sentinel-2 Band 12 (\(2190\text{ nm}\)). Higher values indicate wetter soil and canopy.

Because NSMI relies on optical Sentinel-2 imagery, it is unavailable during monsoon cloud cover (June–September), like NDVI and VCI. During these months, the CDI rests on SPI alone.

docs.title: 3.6b Soil Moisture Index from SAR (SMI)
docs.text:
SMI is derived from Sentinel-1 C-band (\(5.405\text{ GHz}\)) radar backscatter (\(\sigma^\circ_{\text{VV}}\)), normalised against dry and saturated baselines:

\[\text{SMI} = \frac{\sigma^\circ_{\text{VV}} - \sigma^\circ_{\text{dry}}}{\sigma^\circ_{\text{wet}} - \sigma^\circ_{\text{dry}}}\]

Because SAR microwaves penetrate cloud cover, SMI provides all-weather monitoring. It is used in the opt-in thermal formula (config/composite_thermal.yaml) but not in the default cdi-v2026.12 formula.

docs.title: 3.7 Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-1, SPI-3, SPI-6, SPI-12)
docs.text:
Precipitation from UCSB CHIRPS v2.0 (\(0.05^\circ\) grid, daily blended satellite-gauge) is aggregated across rolling windows:

\[A_{k, t} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} P_{t - i}\]
  • SPI-1 (30 days): Detects sudden meteorological dry spells and flash droughts during sowing.
  • SPI-3 (90 days): Primary agricultural metric reflecting full Kharif or Rabi rainfall balance.
  • SPI-6 (180 days): Captures seasonal transition and soil reservoir replenishment.
  • SPI-12 (365 days): Reflects long-term groundwater recharge, reservoir levels, and multi-season hydrological drought.

Cumulative precipitation is fitted to a 2-parameter Gamma distribution \(g(x; \alpha, \beta)\) and transformed to standard normal \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).

docs.title: 3.8 Composite Drought Index (CDI)
docs.text:
CDI integrates meteorological deficit (SPI), vegetation condition (VCI), canopy greenness (NDVI), and surface moisture (NSMI) into a single composite:

\[\text{CDI}_{\text{nominal}} = 0.50 \cdot S(\text{SPI}) + 0.25 \cdot S(\text{VCI}) + 0.15 \cdot S(\text{NDVI}) + 0.10 \cdot S(\text{NSMI})\]

where \(S(I)\) is the normalized severity score (\(0.0 \le S \le 1.0\), where \(1.0\) is extreme drought) for index \(I\). See config/composite.yaml for the authoritative weights and normalisation methods.

docs.title: 1. Evolution of Remote Sensing-Based Drought Monitoring
docs.text:
Drought is a creeping natural hazard characterized by complex, multi-temporal interactions between meteorological precipitation deficits, soil moisture depletion, vegetation physiological stress, and hydrological storage anomalies (Wilhite & Glantz, 1985; Mishra & Singh, 2010).

Historically, drought monitoring in semi-arid tropics relied almost exclusively on ground-based meteorological station networks measuring point rainfall (e.g., India Meteorological Department standard rain gauges). However, ground stations suffer from severe spatial interpolation uncertainties in convective tropical rainfall regimes (McKee et al., 1993; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010).

The advent of satellite Earth Observation (EO) revolutionized drought assessment by providing continuous, spatially exhaustive observations of land surface biophysical parameters:

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                DROUGHT PROPAGATION SEQUENCE                                 |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Atmospheric Circulation Anomaly                                                            |
|         │                                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                                   |
|  Meteorological Drought   ──►  Rainfall Deficit (CHIRPS v2.0, SPI-1 / SPI-3 / SPI-6)        |
|         │                                                                                   |
