docs.title: 2. Benchmark International & National Drought Frameworks
docs.text: Our system is engineered to align strictly with authoritative global and national drought surveillance standards:

docs.title: 2.1 WMO & GWP Standardized Precipitation Index Guidelines
docs.text: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the Global Water Partnership (GWP) established the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) as the definitive global meteorological drought metric (WMO-No. 1090, Standardized Precipitation Index User Guide, 2012). SPI normalizes precipitation accumulations across varying temporal windows (1, 3, 6, 12, 24 months) by fitting a two-parameter Gamma distribution, enabling direct comparisons of dryness across differing climatological regimes.

docs.title: 2.2 U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) Severity Categorization
docs.text:
Developed cooperatively by the USDA, NOAA, and the National Drought Mitigation Center (NDMC) at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Svoboda et al., 2002), the USDM established the percentile-based 5-class severity standard:

\[\text{USDM Classes:}\quad \text{D0 (Abnormally Dry, 20th–30th percentile)} \longrightarrow \text{D4 (Exceptional Drought, } \le \text{2nd percentile)}\]

Our system maps both physical indices and composite indicators directly to this USDM/WMO severity scale, ensuring cross-institutional comparability.

docs.title: 2.3 Indian National Manual for Drought Management (2016)
docs.text:
The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India, promulgated the revised statutory Manual for Drought Management (2016), mandating a multi-criteria trigger mechanism:

  1. Trigger 1 (Mandatory): Rainfall deficiency (SPI or Deviation from Normal \(\le -1.0\)).
  2. Trigger 2 (Impact Indicators): Remote sensing vegetative indices (NDVI/VCI deviation), soil moisture status, and reservoir storage levels.

By integrating CHIRPS SPI, Sentinel-2 VCI, and Sentinel-1 soil moisture into an automated composite, this platform provides direct operational support for Trigger 1 and Trigger 2 scientific verification.

docs.title: 3. Scientific Literature Grounding for Individual Indices
3.1 Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) & Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI)
docs.text:
• Rouse et al. (1974); Tucker (1979): Established NDVI as the normalized contrast between red absorption by chlorophyll-a (\(665\text{ nm}\)) and near-infrared (NIR) scattering by mesophyll cell structures (\(842\text{ nm}\)).
  • Huete et al. (2002): Developed EVI to overcome canopy saturation in high-biomass regimes and minimize soil background brightness in semi-arid sparse vegetation through blue-band atmospheric correction.

docs.title: 3.2 Vegetation Condition Index (VCI)
docs.text:
• Kogan (1990, 1995, 1997): Demonstrated that raw NDVI reflects both climatic fluctuations and local ecological carrying capacity (e.g., irrigated crops vs barren plateau). Kogan introduced VCI to isolate the climatic drought signal by normalizing current NDVI against its multi-year historical minimum and maximum for that specific calendar month.
  • VCI provides a universal \(0\text{--}100\%\) scale, where values \(<40\%\) indicate agricultural drought and \(<20\%\) indicate severe crop failure.

docs.title: 3.3 Temperature Condition Index (TCI) & Vegetation Health Index (VHI)
docs.text:
• Kogan (1995); Karnieli et al. (2010): Demonstrated that vegetation thermal radiance (Land Surface Temperature, LST) rises sharply under soil moisture deficit due to stomatal closure and transpiration cessation. TCI normalizes LST inversely, such that lower TCI values correspond to higher thermal stress.
  • VHI combines VCI and TCI in an equal or weighted balance, reflecting joint moisture and thermal vegetative strain.

docs.title: 3.4 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Soil Moisture (SMI / NSMI)
docs.text: • Ulaby et al. (1982); Wagner et al. (1999); Bauer-Marschallinger et al. (2019): Established the physical sensitivity of C-band SAR backscatter (\(\sigma^\circ\)) to surface soil dielectric permittivity. In cloud-shrouded monsoon regimes where optical sensors fail, Sentinel-1 VV/VH backscatter provides continuous surface soil moisture estimates.

docs.title: 3.5 Composite Drought Indices (CDI) & Re-weighting Theory
docs.text:
• Anderson et al. (2011); Sepulcre-Canto et al. (2012); Hao & AghaKouchak (2013): Proved that univariate drought indices fail to capture joint agricultural-meteorological crises. Composite approaches provide robust, holistic risk detection.
  • Why Random Forest Was Retired: In earlier phases, machine learning classifiers (Random Forest) were explored. However, as documented by Zscheischler et al. (2018) and Rudin (2019), learned black-box classifiers often produce non-monotonic artifacts, uninterpretable predictions during rare out-of-distribution extremes, and lack physical traceability. Our platform retired Random Forest in favor of a transparent, weighted linear composite with dynamic re-weighting under missing components (config/composite.yaml).

docs.title: Dashboard Architecture & Dissemination
docs.text:
The user-facing monitoring system is implemented as a modern full-stack web application built on Next.js, Leaflet, and Supabase.

graph TD
    subgraph Storage ["Cloud Infrastructure (Supabase)"]
        PG["PostgreSQL Database<br/>(Master drought rows & time series)"]
        Bucket["Public Storage Bucket<br/>(GeoJSON boundaries & status JSONs)"]
    end

    subgraph Pipeline ["Python Pipeline Engine"]
        WeeklyJob["Weekly Cron / Pipeline Ingest"] -->|outputs/Dashboard/| Bridge["publish_supabase.py"]

docs.title: 1.1 Python-to-Dashboard Bridge (outputs/Dashboard/)
docs.text: The Python pipeline exports 4 canonical files to outputs/Dashboard/: 1. drought_monitoring_master.csv: Comprehensive master time series of all indices across 954 villages. 2. latest_status.json: High-level operational status, current period, degraded flag, and tehsil summary. 3. data_availability.json: Ingestion audit ledger. 4. processing_manifest.json: Execution run metadata.

docs.title: 1.2 Supabase Publishing (scripts/realtime/publish_supabase.py)
docs.text:
• Server-Side Security: All writes to Supabase execute server-side using the restricted service_role key. The browser client is strictly restricted to read-only access with an anonymous public key.
  • Transactional Row Upsert: New village-months are upserted with conflict resolution on (village_idx, period).

docs.title: 1.3 Next.js Frontend (frontend/)
docs.text:
• Dynamic Leaflet Import: In compliance with Next.js SSR architecture, Leaflet map components are loaded dynamically with { ssr: false } to prevent window is not defined errors.
  • Sub-Second Village Highlighting: Village polygons are rendered via GeoJSON vector tiles with hairline boundaries, interactive hover tooltips, and click-to-filter drilldowns.
  • Recharts Temporal Visualizer: Synchronized charts plot multi-year trends, rainfall deviations, and drought class transitions for any selected village or tehsil.

docs.title: Known Limitations & Error Recovery
docs.text: This document transparently documents known scientific constraints, sensor latency boundaries, and error recovery protocols.

docs.title: 1.1 Tropical Monsoon Cloud Occlusion
docs.text:
• Constraint: During the active southwest monsoon (July–August), dense stratiform and cumulonimbus cloud decks persistently occlude optical sensors.
  • Mitigation: The system fuses Sentinel-1 SAR microwave backscatter (all-weather penetrative capability) and CHIRPS precipitation grids. When optical indices are masked, CDI dynamically drops VCI and re-weights to SPI and SAR soil moisture.

docs.title: 1.2 Missing Archive Years (2019 & 2025)
docs.text:
• Constraint: Historical raw Sentinel-2 raster batches for 2019 and 2025 were missing from the upstream GEE Colab archive export.
  • Handling Rule: Rather than synthesizing or imputing data (which would introduce scientific fraud), the pipeline leaves these optical periods as NaN. CDI is computed from rainfall and soil moisture alone. The frontend renders them as grey "No Data" cells—never zero.

docs.title: 1.3 Sensor Revisit Latency vs Real-Time Claims
docs.text:
• Rule: Never claim real-time when source latency prevents it.
  • Policy: Ingestion from Copernicus and UCSB CHIRPS typically incurs a 3- to 7-day latency. If the latest observation date is older than today, the dashboard status chip displays "degraded" and explicitly shows the actual observation timestamp.

docs.title: 1.4 Spatial Resolution Heterogeneity
docs.text:
• Constraint: Optical Sentinel-2 (\(10\text{--}20\text{ m}\)) and SAR Sentinel-1 (\(10\text{ m}\)) possess fine spatial granularity, whereas CHIRPS v2.0 precipitation operates at \(0.05^\circ\) (\(\approx 5.5\text{ km}\)).
  • Impact: Sub-village rainfall variability is smoothed by the \(0.05^\circ\) precipitation grid. However, downstream vegetative and soil responses captured by Sentinel reflect true micro-topographic and vertisol moisture differences.

docs.title: 2.1 Handling Corrupted Downloads
docs.text: If a raw raster download is interrupted (e.g., incomplete Chrome .crdownload or truncated GeoTIFF): - The ingest scanner verifies GeoTIFF magic bytes and checksums. - Corrupted rasters are flagged in data/dashboard/data_availability.json as failed and skipped. - The pipeline proceeds with the remaining available periods without crashing.

docs.title: 2.2 Recovering from Pipeline Failures
docs.text:
If an unexpected crash occurs during weekly execution: 1. Inspect the processing manifest: outputs/Dashboard/processing_manifest.json. 2. Inspect the latest log in scripts/logs/. 3. Check Supabase connection and service role credentials in .env. 4. Re-run the safe incremental update: 

python scripts/realtime/realtime_update.py
